utterances.text: "... a Serb suffering from tuberculosis for ten years, arrested for looting. The concentration camp/death camp story, having served its purpose, was dropped. But by then the story had already been seen millions of people. The fact that everyone in the photographs of these 'death camps' was well fed just somehow escaped reporters' attention. "At about the same time as the death camp fabrication --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, next page, Mr. Prendergast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "At about the same time as the death camp fabrication was the 'ethnic cleansing' story. While it is true that some Bosnian Serb forces have evicted Muslims from their homes in Serb-held areas, what was not said was that Muslim and Croat forces were carrying out the exact same policy. But the media still presented it as a purely Serbian crime ..." So that's your position at the time on the camps. Do you accept now that there were camps?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what I'm saying here is that -- I mean, that's not my point. The point, as you just read it, was that this was presented as purely a Serbian crime and that the Muslim and Croatian crimes of the exact same nature were suppressed by the media and that there was a demonisation going on of the Serbian people at that time, especially if you take into consideration what's also in this article, that illustrations were being made in leading newspapers like the Chicago Tribune and the New York Times portraying Serbs as pigs, gorillas, vultures. This is all in this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at the foot of this page, if we can, please. And this is the way you put it: "Incredibly, there are even worse examples. On February 5, 1994, there was the infamous Sarajevo market massacre where 68 people were killed. The Serbs were blamed for it, that is until the story leaked out on French TV that the UN knew that the Muslims had bombed their own people in order to induce UN and NATO military involvement. The disgusting ploy worked..." So still your position is it, that the UN knew that the Sarajevo market massacre was --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying there is that the UN -- that some people in the UN knew and that that information was suppressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on to the events after Srebrenica to see how your views may have changed, just help me with this: You volunteered yesterday, and you've put it in writing to be fair to you, that the late Alija Izetbegovic was a war criminal.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nazi war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nazi war criminal, yes. Well, now, it's true that at the age 18 he joined a group that sided with the Germans, but can you just tell us, please, because I may have missed it, what was the actual war crime he committed and that you were so willing to volunteer here? What was it that he actually did?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it was that he was an organiser for the youth movement for the Bosnian Muslim fascist organisation that was helping to recruit Bosnian Muslims for SS divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the -- well, he was part of a movement, and he served a period of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it did. That's what it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked you a specific question: What was his war crime? Because it's very easy to say these things, Mr. Lituchy, but you as a serious historian would know how careful you have to be. What was the war crime he committed?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was a collaborator with an organisation that was recruiting people for the SS divisions in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, at the same part of your evidence, before we move on to one or two of the other things you've said, the same part of your evidence -- let's just see if I can find it -- you volunteered this, and this is -- I have it on page 37200. Having dealt with his being an alleged convicted war criminal and collaborator is how you described it, you went on to say as a result of foreign forces, "These actors again played a role in the persecution of national minorities in Yugoslavia in the 1990s." Now, are you saying that the late President Izetbegovic persecuted national minorities?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what are you identifying as the "persecuted national minorities," then, please?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during his activities as a -- as a Nazi collaborator, there's little doubt that that organisation was involved in the genocide against Serbs, Jews, and Romas in Bosnia during World War II. As far as later on in the 1990s --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That wasn't actually an answer to the question, was it? You volunteered that again, but carry on doing it if you think it's helpful. Now, answer the question, please: Where did he persecute minorities in this 1990s period?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the 1990s, we can say that Izetbegovic was involved in helping to ethnically cleanse parts of the population of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, really? That's it, is it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's enough, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It doesn't occur to you, does it, Mr. Lituchy, that you may see things through a somewhat extraordinary prism, that you hold very one-sided views?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't you? Let's have a look at what you said in the 29th of November 1995. Now, presumably you as a person with an interest in the region had learnt about Srebrenica. Had you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Presumably you as a person interested in the region had learnt about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember when had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that this article has to have in mind that you're now aware of this. The detail of it wasn't necessarily known but the generality of it was known, this most appalling event. Let's see what you then expressed about the Dayton pact. If we just go a little bit further down the page, please. "The Dayton Pact --" third line -- "like the Munich Pact nearly 60 years ago, is not a peace agreement, but rather a prelude to further war. The Dayton Pact signifies the unconditional surrender by the Bosnian Serb leaders to the neocolonial powers of the West, led by the United States. In one of the most obscene spectacles of fascist thuggery in modern times, the Clinton regime has imposed its neocolonial political and military rule over the destinies of some 20 million people in the Balkans by staging a dubious international conference inside a military base in Ohio. It represents one of the greatest setbacks to human rights since the Vietnam War." Help us. Is this a paragraph that you're happy to live with?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And against which your position as a serious academic should be measured?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I certainly -- I certainly believe that the facts do prove that the war -- the wars that occurred in Yugoslavia were unnecessary and would not have occurred without the US determination to break up the country, yes. There's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's the terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go on two pages, please, Mr. Prendergast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that wasn't your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question to you was - and if you want it again you're welcome to it: Is this a view to which you hold and against which your position as a serious academic should be measured?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say it should be, should it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you said that that -- well, I won't quibble with you, but I've made clear that that's the basis for my position then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at how you describe things two pages on. "There were several important tactical objectives that had to be accomplished first before the US could directly impose its political and economic jackboot on the peoples of the Balkans. Among these, some are quite obvious: the restoration of the fascistic movements among the Croatian and Bosnian Muslim population calling for secession from Yugoslavia; the international recognition of these fascistic secessionist movements and the destruction of a unified socialist Yugoslav state; a policy of war against those who were against this (the Serbs); the demonisation of the Serbs through a media campaign launched by governments, public relations firms and human rights organisations which staged 'atrocities' that never happened ..." Now, you understand, Mr. Lituchy, we're examining you as a -- for reliability, for integrity and objectivity. Can you tell us, please, what were the staged atrocities that you had in mind so shortly after Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't remember exactly which ones I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us a collection then.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I certainly can refer you to a couple that occurred after this, including Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not going to be very much use, is it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, please listen. You as a serious academic seeking to influence - let's not beat about the bush - world events, assert following the Dayton Peace Accord that you know many regarded as a good solution, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you assert that there have been staged atrocities. Now, please, you wrote it, you tell us what it meant.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I can recall one in particular. There was the article that appeared in The New York Times about 50.000 rapes. That's one that certainly strikes -- that I can recall that I must have had in mind. The fact that this story of mass rapes was being bandied about and yet there was very little evidence, if any at all, of any unusually high level of rapes at all, in fact, compared to, say, in the United States in a normal year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: English is your natural language. This is in English. False account of rapes over a period of time is an allegation that can always be made, but "staged atrocity" in the mouth of an educated academic --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I have one. I'm sure I have one in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, please think about it.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had one in mind but unfortunately at this moment I can't recall exactly what I had in mind when I wrote that because I didn't come here to testify because about my -- all of my writings. I can't remember every single one of my writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any chance you were thinking about Srebrenica or something like that?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's read on. "... that never happened while distorting the conflict; the imposition of UN --"

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nice. So that was what you were getting at, that you suggest that I had said that Srebrenica was a staged atrocity? Do you have evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll press on with questions. It's not for you to ask me questions. You've been given an opportunity to explain your writings.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "... while distorting the conflict; the imposition of UN sanctions and 'peacekeepers' as a military stalling tactic, to hold the Serbs back militarily while the Croats and Muslims were covertly armed; the corruption and splitting of the Serbian leadership, pitting the Bosnian Serb leaders against the government in Belgrade by making phoney deals with both sides; sending the CIA and Pentagon war machine into Croatia and Bosnia to covertly train and arm the Croats and Muslims while collecting intelligence on the Serbs ..." Just that sentence. Where did you source there, so we can know?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall that. I can recall that I sourced that first of all in an article in the Independent about Clinton's armed -- I mean, you know, we're really asking me particulars about articles that I wrote ten -- about ten years ago, but I do remember this, as a matter of fact, that there was an article in the Independent that I -- that I was referring to in this -- in this line here, about arm shipments to the Muslims that Clinton -- the Clinton administration had in fact coordinated secretly, breaking the arms embargo, as a matter of fact. And this is prior to Dayton, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the next sentence and I'm done with this page and I've only got one more article I'm going to have the time to ask you about, I think, today. Let's look at the next sentence to the end of the paragraph: "... the NATO bombing and the coordinated Croat and Muslim offences and genocidal attacks on civilian populations."

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're been very free with the use of the word "genocide" since you've been here. Which of the genocidal attacks are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the -- the definition of crimes of genocide, as I understand it, is that when a government or -- or army partakes in the attempted destruction of a people, either in part or in full, by carrying out certain actions against the civilian population, that that constitutes a crime of genocide. There's no -- there's no question in my mind that there were actual bombings of civilian targets in -- during the 1990s by the Clinton administration. This was confirmed by every investigation, every serious investigation that's been done on the subject, and therefore it -- it constitutes if that -- it can be argued that a crime of genocide was committed if the attempt was to destroy the Serbian civilian population in either Bosnia or Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, so that the Court can know where -- what your position is, name us one of these -- and it must be intentionally, presumably, bombing of a civilian target so we can just have it in mind.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. Can you name for us one of those civilian targets subject to what must have been an intentional bombing.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999 in -- during our delegation's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is 1995, so we're looking at anything before 29th of November, 1995, Mr. Lituchy.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I read in the newspapers at that time when I -- prior to writing this article, was that there were hospitals in Bosnia that -- civilian hospitals for Serbian people that were being bombed by NATO. That's what I -- that's what I read at the time, and that was the basis of my -- of my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Newspaper article, hospital bombing. Thank you. Last sentence: "The final nail in the coffin was the complete surrender of the current Serb leaderships in both Belgrade and Bosnia to the demands of US imperialism." So you thought the compromise made by the Serb leadership and RS and also in Belgrade completely wrong, did you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any diplomatic agreement based on bombing can be considered valid or legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go and see, for the last extract, which I think will help us with an understanding of you, to this document of June 28, 1999. History department at Kingsborough Community College, headed The American Barbarism and the Big Lie Technique. And if we just go on, please, to page 4 of 4, Mr. Prendergast, and see where you've summarised.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is this from? I don't believe I've seen this, but anyway...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: History department, Kingsborough --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is not published by the history department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom is it published?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, Mr. Nice. How would I know?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please receive this document? I expected to get another one too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you should have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judge Robinson, may I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, do you have copies for --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I have copies for everybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although, as I say, I'm quite happy to just have it on the record, I'm neutral as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO. Mr. Lituchy, what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to this cross-examination, you directed me not to answer questions that were not directly related to the facts about which I've been called to testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, these questions go to your credibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document is headed American Barbarism and The Big Lie Technique. The original location is set out there.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not published by the history department of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom was it published?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I actually don't know. I haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is attributed to you.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may very well have been written by me but it certainly is not published by who it says it's published by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just check to see that --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who published this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just check to see whether the first paragraph appears to be your position. Let's go to the first paragraph. I hadn't intended to but I will. "Is there anyone left who still leaves that Yugoslavia was destroyed by 'ancient ethnic hatreds,' and not from without by Western - particularly American - imperialism and covert action?" This would appear to be your position, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we go to the fourth page of four and see what is attributed to you and I'm going to ask you if you adopt this as your terminology. Halfway down that first paragraph, we see this: "The defeat of the Serbs leaves us all with a much more dangerous world." That's no doubt your view. "It has fully exposed the dark, criminal nature of William Jefferson Clinton - a rapist, a murderer, a gangster and a fascist - and his entire government. But we should not compare Clinton to Hitler; it does not do justice to the full range of Clinton's social pathology. He's best compared to a Ted Bundy or a John Wayne Gacey ..." You'll see where it ends. If you go to the last paragraph on this page, this: "We must promise ourselves to do better this time than after Jasenovac." We know your interest in Jasenovac. It goes on: "We must promise ourselves that there will be a reckoning for the crimes committed by American fascism, and that there will be a punishment extracted - in blood if need be..." These your words, Mr. Lituchy?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who is guilty of crimes of genocide, yes, of course. Of course. This is -- if -- if these are the crimes committed, then someone should be published for those crimes. I believe -- I'm not opposed to the death penalty, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things then: The description of Clinton and the comparison between him and Hitler is one you still stand by, is it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many -- there are many comparisons to be made, and the fact that both Hitler and Clinton tried to divide a unified Yugoslav state and did so by promoting proxy armies that included fascists among them, yes, absolutely. This is -- this is a very clear analogy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's not beat about the bush. You're saying here in terms, so that we can follow you, as the serious historian you are, you're saying here that Clinton is worse than Hitler. Is that really your view?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that Hitler was guilty of sexual crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's your answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my -- that's my answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just conclude then with focusing again on the last paragraph and indeed the last words that I read out. "We must promise ourselves that there will be a reckoning for the crimes committed by American fascism and that there will be a punishment extracted - in blood if need be..." What were you seeking to achieve by publishing, saying, broadcasting, whatever it was, that sort of observation?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know who published this. I made that clear before. I mean, stand by these words. I think I did write this. I don't know actually who published it, but I do believe I did write it, yes. So let's correct that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What shedding of blood, did you, Mr. Lituchy --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see, I see. I see what you're saying. I've already answered that question. I explained to you that I believe that the death penalty is appropriate in crimes of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's shedding of blood, is it? Forgive me, I know there are various brutal ways of killing people effected in various States in the United States of America but I'm not sure that any of them sheds blood. Do correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's more of a metaphor for the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it, or are you lying to us?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because by shedding blood -- Yes, lying, Mr. Lituchy.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because by "shedding blood" you meant something entirely different from the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's absurd. But I will add this, I will add this: That people deserve to be defended against crimes of genocide that they -- and that may entail the shedding of blood, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's have it: Is it the death penalty or is it the shedding of blood?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Both. Very well. What shedding of blood did you envisage in 1999 - I have the date again - as being justified, assuming that the date --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defending people from crimes of genocide just precisely as the crimes that I've documented here with the Romas and other refugees from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you realise the significance of the date, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date? I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is -- the date this is June the 28th 1999. So that's just --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall -- I don't think that date is valid or is accurate. I'm not sure when the date of this piece is because I didn't publish it, but I do believe I -- somehow someone got a hold of this. I may have written this, or I -- I'm really not sure. I don't know where this comes from. You never told me where you got this from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, we can only do our best with the Internet and we can --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the Internet a reliable source? I think I'm more reliable than the Internet. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, you confirmed that the Internet is reliable because you confirmed that these are your words and we took it off it. We can only as to the date of the publication what the Internet provides.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The description is false.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The description is straight out false, so this is not valid. It was not published by any -- by the history department of Kingsborough College, so that's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, do you have anything to do with the Communist Party of Australia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very good question Judge Kwon. That's a very good question. I don't even know -- I don't even know anything about the Communist Party of Australia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The address at the bottom of the page says that it seems to be related to that institution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know. I -- I -- I've never even heard of the Communist Party of Australia. I assume there may very well be one but I don't they anything about it. I don't know the first thing about it, the Communist Party of Australia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I turn now to the reliability of your interviews? First of all, and I deal with this swiftly and compendiously, the document that we have before us and as -- I'm not sure what decision the Court has made but I'm focusing on pages 1 to 45 and 127 until the end of tab 1 because it seems to me that the other part hadn't been spoken to and tab 2 has been expressly not produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's an accurate representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had no investigator and no particular investigative skills. How did you choose your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for -- we -- I don't recall exactly how we found her but we -- through my contacts in Belgrade I asked for an interpreter for these interviews. That's the best I can remember as far as that's concerned. I believe it was through one of my colleagues in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it occur to you that the interpreter might herself, as it turned out to be, have views and interpose her judgement between question and answer?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that -- I agree that was, regrettably, something we couldn't quite control. We tried to stop her from doing that but we didn't want -- we didn't want her to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So do you accept, do you, in the way that I think His Honour Judge Robinson observed, it was clear she wasn't doing straight translation because she -- she leapt in before questions were completed and sometimes gave very short answers where there had been a great deal of speech from the person being spoken to.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the translations were a fair and accurate representation of what people were saying, but it is also true -- you see it doesn't have to be either/or, Mr. Nice. It can be -- it's both. It's both the fact that the translations were accurate and fair representations of what people were saying and also that she interposed things that she had no right and no business interposing, and it was very annoying to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked you if this was the serious work of scholarship, as it were -- I didn't use the word "scholarship." You confirmed that it was serious work. If you knew certainly before coming to this court that what she had said was not free of her own intervention, why did you not arrange for the transcript to be properly transcribed by an independent -- sorry, why did you not arrange for the tape to be properly transcribed by an independent and neutral interpreter?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually I didn't know that I was going to be -- I didn't make this transcript for this Court, but I did -- had I been more aware of when I was going to -- if I was going to testify, when I was going to be -- when I was going to testify -- I didn't have the time or the resources at the time to -- to do that. But yes, I absolutely did want to do that and I think it -- it was certainly on my agenda to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the event, and unless the matter had been drawn to the Court's attention, both by the accused and by me, this transcript would have gone in without correction, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you draw to our attention that it was false?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I thought you said would I have. Yes, I would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, did you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was already -- it was brought up immediately by President Milosevic before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coincidentally while you use the term "President Milosevic," it reminds me: I've only been able to research so much of your material from open sources, and I may have missed it, but your Serb -- your personal Serbian background isn't referred to in any of your public writings?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's because I'm not a Serbian nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you not think when seeking to change world events by expression of opinions in the way that you do that it might have been preferable and fairer to reveal that you have a Serb historical connection?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that that's necessary. I don't think -- I don't think one has to identify what one's national -- one's ancestors are. The human race originated in Africa. We're all Africans too. I mean, we can't -- it would be extremely unfair and it's not -- it's certainly no scientific requirement that one identify one's ethnic heritage in any kind of writing or research. I've never heard of such a -- such an idea before actually. This is -- this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, how far back does your Serb ancestry go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a native-born US citizens. My parents are native-born US citizens. Two of my grandparents are of Serbian background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, you had wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to put Mr. Nice right. He said that you drew attention to the problem with the translation in the transcript. I drew attention to the translation, the problems with the translation, and precisely that was the reason that I emphasised that the exhibit I'm tendering is the tape and not the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transcript, which has serious defects. And I'm sure you'll be able to find that passage in the transcript of my having said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I give you full credit for that, Mr. Milosevic. What Mr. Nice attributed to me was also accurate. Mr. Nice, we have to take a break now, and we'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question for technical reasons? Is Mr. Nice going to finish before the end of business today so that I can know for my next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next session is how long?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Seventy minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seventy minutes. I would certainly hope to finish before the next session. I know the topics I have to deal with. There are only about two in the nature of things because amongst other things I want to point you to some of the shortcomings of the transcript. It will be closer to the end of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, we'll go through your document in broad fashion, please, just to remind ourselves what it amounts to. Pages 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 there is preface we haven't focused on that, I'm not going to trouble you with it. Page 8 is a press release. Again, I'm not interested in that. Page 9 and in between pages 9 and 13 we have an interview with Bratislava Morina. Now as a matter of history, Bratislava Morina is the wife, or was the wife, now widow of Rrahman Morina, who replaced Vllasi when he was forced out of office, didn't she? Didn't he, rather.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And her husband, or her late husband, was indeed a fully loyal supporter of this accused and indeed -- well, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was brought in to replace Vllasi when Vllasi's independence of mind was troublesome, yes?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that part I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because this is not a woman I've been able to make any contact with, I'm not going to ask you any questions about the content of what she says because I can't deal with it save just for this: You say that you had no cooperation with or assistance, I think, by ministry bodies or by Serb bodies in your inquiry, but if you go to page 12, please --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, wait a second. You're misrepresenting what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, if I'm misunderstanding it, you must put us right, because it's quite clear from page 12, in the middle of the page, that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is entirely at your disposal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the interviews of refugees. That's precisely what I was talking about, that's what I was questioning about. We did not receive any help from the government in that regard, no. But as far as other -- yes, we did have some, we did have assistance as far as some of the other interviews, but not with the refugees, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed when -- if we look on the same page, page 12 a little further down, "Lituchy: I think we would like to visit a refugee camp, if that's possible, particularly a refugee camp that was hit by NATO bombing." That was something, what, that the Foreign Ministry or Ministry of Refugees --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't organise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They didn't?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But they were prepared to do anything they could to help you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I'd agree with that but because they didn't help us as far as the refugees were concerned. I mean, it's true -- I mean, I don't want to -- with all respect to Mrs. Morina, I don't -- you know, I -- but still we didn't get any help as far as interviewing the refugees, no. That's definite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were known, however, wherever you went as being an investigation that was against NATO; correct?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And associated with the then Serb government; correct?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not necessarily, no. That's not necessarily true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To be against NATO would be to be siding, in a simple analysis of events, with the Serb government, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that that's too simple, yes, you're right. It's a simplification of -- I mean, it's very possible to be opposed to the NATO bombing and still not be in support of President Milosevic. In fact, many of -- there were many people in our delegation who had that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a historian, you know that sources and -- sources are critical to the work of a historian?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if -- if you have two sources, one better than another, you go to the best --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- not to the second best. If something is to your knowledge in need of checking, you check it.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although it remains a fact that this record was something you knew needed checking but never was checked.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which record are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The record of interviews that we're going to look at. You knew it needed checking because you knew that the interpreter was not doing the job of interpreting faithfully and yet you didn't actually check what was on the transcription, did you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, well, there's a reason, there's an explanation for that. What happened was that the transcript -- the transcription was done by a colleague of mine in Ohio who also had a translator helping him to improve the translation. I thought perhaps all of these problems would be worked out. They weren't, and shortly after that I became -- I was very ill for a period of about three years, actually, after this took place, so I was unable really to devote any time at all. I -- I -- I was undergoing chemotherapy and I was very sick. I couldn't -- I had no time for this during the three years after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, when did you first then become aware that the problems hadn't been sorted?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When exactly? Well, I certainly knew that the original translation needed to be improved. So I -- in that regard, I can -- I can tell you that I knew from the beginning that we needed a better, a complete and improved translation. However, as I've said all along, I still maintain that this transcript fairly represents the content of these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure how you can do that, you see, because you realised it was in need of correction, it was dealt with by a colleague of yours and another translator --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you think that he'd corrected all the problems?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he corrected 99 per cent of the problems at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you know he hadn't done a completely satisfactory job?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did find -- I did find one or two things after I published it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is that, because you speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do speak and understand -- read some Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you've actually listened to the tapes?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since your unfortunate ill health and treatment and coming here to give evidence, and you knew that the tape and the transcript were not accurate reflections one of the other.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you realise that the -- from the very beginning our main purpose was to conduct the interviews and do so on video and thereby preserving the full integrity of those interviews on videotape, and therefore it was always possible -- I suppose I'm guilty of not showing a sufficient amount of -- of speed and -- and effort in -- in providing a better transcript. I should say that there were only 200 copies of this report published in 2000, and it was by no means meant for a broad --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to cut you short because I want to finish my cross-examination in under 50 per cent of the time.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think you did. I simply said to you -- this Court is dealing with very serious matters and I said to you you came here knowing that the tape and the transcript were not accurate reflections one of the other.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tape. The tape is accurate. The videotape is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shan't take any more time on that. Pages 15 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the inaccuracy relates to the transcript, the translation, not the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The translation of the transcript, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look between pages 15 and 27 -- 28, beg your pardon, we'll find something that relates, I think, all to people leaving after the bombing, with refugees -- beg your pardon, this relates to refugees in Serbia and their condition, and I'm not going to focus on that at all. So if we can go to page 30. Now, these refugees, Mr. Lituchy, you would accept are going to be either extremely difficult or impossible for me to find in the short period of time that I've had your documents?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made no efforts to contact them before allowing their answers to be given as in evidence this case, did you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know perfectly well, if they were refugees, that tracking them down with little more than one name or sometimes a couple of names and a former address is going to be extremely difficult if not impossible?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. As to these pages, I remind you of an answer you gave I think to His Honour Judge Robinson but it may have been elsewhere, where the word KLA was not on the tape but was on the transcript. Do you remember that? And you said, well, it doesn't really much matter because the implication was that the KLA were the people involved.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the answer to my question, the Roma refugee made it clear that they were armed Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, and "armed Albanians," therefore, can be transliterated, for convenience of reading, to "KLA"?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claim -- I did not do that but it's -- as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the document before the Court is to be reliable, such errors ought to have been corrected, oughtn't they?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's why I brought the videotape as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that if we now look at -- if we look on page 30 we've got Nenezu, Abazi, and then on page 31 we've already looked at the one reference at the top where I'm suggesting to you that the word KLA was never mentioned, line 3. Halfway down the page in the answers of Tefiq I understand that the word again "KLA" has simply been added to the text. Inexcusable really, isn't it? It's your report, but it's inexcusable.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that. I don't know what the answer to that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, you're a historian. You tell us you're a serious historian. You've confirmed that the sources have to be checked, you've confirmed that this needed to be checked and wasn't checked. It's your discipline. If you present a report about things done by the KLA purporting to be a transcript of what people say knowing that that material is being given in evidence, it is inexcusable not to correct an error of the kind I've described.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me a question or making a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly am asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not inexcusable because I brought the videotape which is the full interview in its entirety, and that -- if -- if I was trying to dissemble or trying to distort anything, I certainly would not have done -- I would not have brought the original with me and presented that. That's -- that's the basis of my interviews. That's what we intended to do and that's -- that should be looked upon as the most important evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These witnesses -- not these witnesses, these people being interviewed were found for you by --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't hear -- what's the question? I didn't hear the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: People interviewed were found for him, but he denies that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to a place where refugees -- are you talking about the Romas and Egyptians? You're talking about Egyptians and Romas, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This part of your report, yes.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought. No. This is an area in which refugees were living. This was an area that had already, prior to the time of the refugee crisis, had been a place where Romas and Egyptians were living, and so this is where the refugees fled to. Now, as you -- if you look at the -- if you look at the original tapes or CDs, whatever you have, you can see for yourself that people came. They were -- they came, they heard perhaps secondhand or thirdhand, that people were -- that people from other countries were there to interview refugees and so they showed -- they stepped forward. They stepped forward on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this page, page 32 of your transcript, we'll find, will we not when we see the original properly and fully translated, that your interpreter was gathering people out of the crowd or gathering people and calling them forward to come and speak to you. Is that the role she took?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not a fair representation. Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not in the transcript, it's on the tape.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the tape. No, I don't think that's a fair representation of what she was doing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we move on to page 35, please, very quickly, and you'll see a third of the way down the page -- and if there's a spare copy I'm happy for Mr. Prendergast to lay it on the overhead projector if it makes it more interesting for those viewing but not to delay us. We see a third of the way down the page, "The children awake at night calling 'mama, mama.' I have nothing to give them. They are afraid of aeroplanes." Aeroplane is pretty important, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you show me where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A third of way down page 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you sure it's 35?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Reference to aeroplanes is important, isn't it, because aeroplanes connect it to NATO.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's specifically important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why was it added then to what the person said, because as I understand it, and I'm dependent --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to me. -- unhappily so, on Ms. Kisic, who has given up her weekend to listen to the tapes and attempt to help me. The words "aeroplane" doesn't feature on the original tape. To add "aeroplanes" would be inexcusable, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question, as I understand it, was is that necessary -- is that very important to the -- as I recall that's what you asked me: Is this very important to this testimony? No, it's not, because I'll tell you why -- what this is about. This is about how these children, the Roma children, were being persecuted. This is the -- this is the extent of the horrible nature of crimes, is that children were being killed, children were being raped, and children were being persecuted. Children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 37, please. Third line down, one of your colleagues, I think: "Why do you think they were doing this?" Answer from Berisha now: "The Albanian soldiers did that to us because we support Serbia and we oppose secession." Well, which bit of that last six words is important? "We support Serbia" or "We oppose secession"? Is it one bit that's important or both?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it is important because -- I'm not sure -- you may be trying to say that this is not in the tape, and I'm not sure about that right off the top of my head. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're quite right I'm going to suggest that one bit of it isn't in the tape, but I want you to tell me which bits are important. Serbia or secession is important?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then why did somebody add the words "we oppose secession" when those words were never there?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this remotely a serious minded work of scholarship or research or was this political material?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is -- it is important because we wanted to know what the relationship of the Romas was and -- was to the Yugoslav government. That was -- that was -- and so when Romas did tell us that they served in the Yugoslav military or if they supported the Yugoslavia, if they considered that to be their state and they considered it to be defending them prior to the bombing, then it was -- yes, then it would be important. If that's an error, I -- I deeply regret that that's -- that that's there if that's in error, but I don't think that that in any way compromises the entirety of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look down the page, please. About seven lines up from the bottom. Rakipi: "On June 26 we left Kosovo after the KLA forced us from our home." I'm going suggest to you that the word "KLA" doesn't feature there. And similarly, if we go to page 38, please, about 12 lines down, in the answer of Eles or Elis: "I left Kosovo on June the 26th. After I left Kosovo, KLA soldiers took everything." Again the words "KLA" were not included. That's the sort of error I think that you accept, with your recollection, happened, don't you? "KLA" was inserted where "KLA" was not said.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if we move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm not doing all points, Your Honours, just a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we move on to page 44 so that we can have in advance of the translation some understanding of how these interviews were conducted. If we look down the page about seven lines to your answer, "Thank you and we wish you the best," had you, although it's not included on the transcript, asked for someone who had had a family member killed and who had witnessed that to come forward and speak and then --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then we go on to page 47, and as I've already indicated between 47 and 126 there's been no evidence given and I forecast we won't be dealing with them. We then come to 127 where the interviewees were in the basement of the hotel and where may have been afforded protective measures so that their names mustn't be given. We're calling them really 1, 2 and 3, Albanians 1, 2, and 3. And at page 127 we are on Albanian number 1. Before I look at these to the extent that I must, help me with this: Remember I said if you have a source of information that is good but not necessarily the best, the appropriate course for a historian is to go to the best, and you accepted that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This morning you knew something before the accused mentioned it or before it was discussed in court of what had been said on the last occasion about contacts made by someone on my behalf with Albanian number 3. How did you learn about that, about what had passed in court concerning my inquiries or inquiries conducted on my behalf for Albanian number 3?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never -- I didn't know. I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The process whereby an investigator had spoken to Albanian number 3, are you saying you knew nothing of that?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard you said -- say -- that much I heard you say in court when I was here last week. That I heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you had no other knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other knowledge. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, I don't have time to check the actual transcript of what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Bear in mind the Prosecutor is not pursuing that. He's not pursuing that, so there's no need to address it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 127, then, we're with Albanian number 1. Halfway down the page you asked: "Did this political party run in the previous elections ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, unless I am advised otherwise, it doesn't seem to me necessary to go into closed session to read out the answer. In any event, the Chamber will remember that I had achieved some contact with this individual last week. I propose to read the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer says this: "No, this is a new political party, formed only last year, so we haven't yet run in elections. This was the one, the only Albanian party to stand by the government, and our political position was for Kosovo and Metohija to stay in Yugoslavia and to organise humanitarian aid for people, and to oppose secession." Now, can you explain to me why, if it's the case, that answer is completely incorrectly transcribed in two ways? First, no reference of "opposing secession," and secondly, what was actually said on the tape was that it was the only political party to stay with the people during the NATO airstrikes, saying nothing whatsoever about standing by the government. Can you explain to me, please, if this is a serious work of scholarship, why there should be -- or research, why there should be those two errors?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as I remember, the interpreter in the film said it was "President Milosevic" instead of "the government." So "Albanian party to stand by President Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must say that I've noted that also, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like -- I wanted to ask the witness why it was changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just check? The reference to Milosevic, I hadn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Different conscientious ears pick up different things but I'm not going to challenge that what Your Honours heard may have been different qualities of sound,, and that would also need explaining. So perhaps should I ask the question or would Your Honour prefer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, one of two possibilities is that there was no reference to either government or President Milosevic, and the other is that there is a reference to Milosevic, all of which mistranslated as standing by the government. Can you explain why those changes would have been made, either of them?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't, but if it does say they're supporting President Milosevic, that is in essence the same thing as supporting the government in this regard. In this case, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now if we look at page 128, and to remind everybody this is the meeting in the basement of the hotel with people sat on a table and, as you've told us, lots of people there -- or not lots of people, other people there. Last line on page 128, and it shouldn't go on the overhead protector, sorry, take it away. The questioner asks how many people were forced out by the KLA, and an answer is given of 150.000 Albanians. But in fact if one listens to the tape, somebody in the group of others volunteered the number. Isn't that right? And then maybe the person being interviewed gave it himself.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think the correct thing to do is look at the tape. If you want -- if you want to get to the truth, that's what you have to do and that's why I brought the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remember I asked you questions about the advantages of interviewing people singly and you explained the advantage of having people in -- other people there? You were there.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the rigor of the interview process such that if somebody from the crowd, as it were, or from the other people there, said 150.000, the person being interviewed would say, okay, 150.000. Is that actually what was going on?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This -- this would be a mistake from the transcription from the tape, if that is indeed a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The suggestion is that this information is volunteered by someone else and it's then perhaps picked up by the person being interviewed, put in the answer, but of course it doesn't come from him, it comes from the crowd. Is that the rigor of your interviewing process made real?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You're conflating what happened in the transcription with the process of the interview, which is -- which is really a distortion. You're distorting -- you're distorting the truth. That's not what happened. I did not -- I did not say this is -- this is the answer. Someone in the crowd says something, that's the answer. This is something that happened from -- this is why we have the videotape here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go on to page 132. It is Albanian number 2. And halfway down the page again: "Lituchy: Were you threatened by anyone in Kosovo? "Ismali: Yes, because I supported --" says Yugoslavia -- "and I opposed secession." Again I'm going to suggest to you that the reference to secession is simply not there on the sound track. Do you allow for the possibility that whoever is responsible for the transcript has been adding little answers about secession, opposition to secession, regularly?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I allow that -- about something that I -- some hypothesis. I guess I have to allow for a hypothesis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, you're in a slightly better position than a hypothesis. It's your tape, you've listened to it, and you speak Serbian. So tell us, because we're going to eventually have a transcript, do you allow for the possibility that in the overall process for which you are responsible references to secession were added to what was said by witnesses -- not witnesses --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I allow for that possibility? It's -- if it's -- if that's what happened, I guess I have to allow for it. I mean, you're -- you're asking me questions about -- the answers to which I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more of these and then I think I'm done on this topic. When we come to page 138, we're on Witness number -- not witness, Albanian number 3. Perhaps we ought to look at -- perhaps you could look at page 130 -- 133 first, where we're still on Albanian number 2. And there's -- in the middle of the page there's a question, "Under what conditions do you think you might be able to return to Kosovo?" And the answer given is: "If our army and police return to Kosovo, we'll go the same day." Now, if the man actually said as recorded, "When it's safe to live there and work there, I'll go," can you explain why the reference to the army and the police has been added?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he did say that, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 134, towards the foot of the page, and now we are with Albanian number 3. Albanian number 3 was described as a traitor, and we know, indeed the accused confirmed it himself, that it was the word "tradesman." Can you explain how the word "traitor" could have been typed in there?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was brought up last week, I thought about it and I think that what must have happened, and this again must have been a problem in the -- either in the translation during the interview or during the translation during the transcription, that the transcriber heard the word "traitor" and it was "trader" and not "traitor," and misheard, misheard. Now, that's -- that's my guess. That's my best guess since I didn't do the transcription.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go up three or four lines to the third line of this answer, where it says: "Until the NATO bombing, I loved and sympathised with democracy in the United States."

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Same page, just three lines up. Four or five lines up. "Until the NATO bombing, I loved and sympathised with democracy ..." If the tape can only be heard -- reveals his saying, "Until recently I loved and sympathised with democracy in the United States ..." any reason why it should have been changed to "until the NATO bombing"?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally, please, page 135, still with Albanian number 3. If we look halfway down the page at this: "Do you know what torture methods the KLA use?" Albanian number 3 replies, "What more do you want? They're killing people. They killed them by strangulation and by torture." Could there be any reason for adding those words "they killed them by strangulation and by torture" when the words weren't said at all?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall -- I do recall remembering that that was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You recall that that was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I do because I just looked at the -- I just looked at the -- no, just the addition. I remember him saying what more do you not want that they're killing people, but I recall just -- which was listening to the tapes in the hotel last week looking at them that it was -- that that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mean the mistake was there?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I mean, these are very dramatic words. "Killing people by strangulation and torture." Did you really not think you owed any duty to correct the material being presented to this court?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I owed a duty to correct the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why didn't you present it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I present the tapes which have the original--

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, come, come, Mr. Lituchy. You saw the muddle we got into with the tapes. You knew that this printed document was being presented.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There shouldn't have been any muddle with the tapes. The tapes are in good condition. They do appear to be in much worse condition than as I brought them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that this document not just for reasons of its method of preparation is an unreliable document and that your answers today show that. It's nothing like the sort of material you as an historian should be relying on, is it? It's flawed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has flaws, but it correct -- I think it -- I think it accurately presents for the most part what these refugees had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now I'm going to turn to the other shortcomings of your interview and I want to suggest to you that what you're now going to see is a proper exercise of research if viewed objectively. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents concerned are the subject of protective measures so we can't put them on the overhead projector but with the Court's leave I'll deal with this in public session because I think it's appropriate that can, and that I should. And I'm going to ask the witness to have before him two documents, one a statement of Mr. Sutch, and if he has that one first. You would accept, wouldn't you Mr. Lituchy, that secondhand evidence, that is evidence of A saying what B said is often not as good as first-hand evidence, what B said himself?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that here what you have is the witness statement of the investigator who contacted Albanian number 3. I'm not going to take you through all of it but I am going to take you to just one passage. If you look down towards the end of the first page you will see a paragraph that begins, and we don't use the name of the person, "... stated that invariably that," Albanian number 1 --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the foot of the first page. So we're going to use code. So Albanian number 3 stated that another person was present in the interviews: "As well as plainclothes Serbian Interior Ministry police officers. He does not recall police being present at the Hotel Prague interview. He believes that he was identified as an interview subject ..." and so on. Now, if you read those two lines together carefully, they coming from an interview conducted over the telephone with an interpreter, there is some ambiguity in there, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was presence of police officers but he doesn't recall them being present in the Hotel Prague. Would you accept that the appropriate thing to do, if possible, is go and take a statement, find out exactly what the person meant to say?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's fine, but this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now look at the next statement, if you would be so good, remembering again that we aren't going to identify the person at all. It's now in numbered paragraphs and as you can see from the name at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's coming to the Chamber immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you can see, incidentally, that the date of the statement was the 13th of March. You can see that it is an interview if you look at the details with the place of the interview, the interviewer, the interpreter identified. A one-to-one interview subject to the necessary presence of interpreters. And without going through all of it, the person interviewed, Albanian number 3, explains this: "On the 28th of June, 1999, the building was stormed by many Kosovo Albanians and at the same time British NATO troops entered the premises ... The situation became chaotic and I, together with --" I won't read that out -- "left with the assistance of others. That day I travelled to Belgrade where I remained until the end of August 1999," and then refers to the circumstances of return and family matters. Paragraph 4 sets out his own employment history. Paragraph 5: "I recall taking part in many interviews during the period in Belgrade, but I am unable to remember all of them individually. The interviews concerned NATO aggression and its consequences, why Kosovo Albanians were leaving the region of Kosovo and support of the Milosevic policy on Kosovo. I do not know who the interviews were arranged by, but I was aware that they were conducted with the approval of the Belgrade authorities probably for propaganda purposes." Well, of course your interviews in Belgrade at that time were conducted with the approval of Belgrade authorities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about the cooperation you had with the ministry?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which ministry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The ministry we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The refugee -- Ministry for Refugees?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not organise these interviews, Mr. Nice. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but this statement is not truthful. It's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not accurate or not truthful?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not accurate. I'm not -- he does say that -- he does say here in the statement, if I can get back to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're sticking with this statement?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we're going to see exactly what he says?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says: "I do not know who the interviews were arranged by but I was aware that they were conducted with the approval of the Belgrade authorities and probably for propaganda purposes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You want to say that that's --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that can't be -- that's not accurate, and I wonder whether that's actually -- if that's maybe under duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And against whom would you like to assert duress, Mr. Lituchy?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not asserting -- I'm not asserting anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
