utterances.text: But you just have. You said you wonder if it's under duress.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wonder if there isn't the pressure of perhaps the threat of being put out to the wolves, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which wolves?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who would put him to the wolves?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or the KLA? This is a person interviewed for the purpose of dealing with your testimony, Mr. Lituchy.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not truthful, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not truthful. Very well. That's the assertion you are --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the truth, that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The interviews were generally conducted by Serbian journalists. Let's turn over to paragraph 6: "I recall one interview in particular sometime in July or August 1999, which took place in the basement of the Hotel Prague in Belgrade and that was conducted in the English language and I responded to questions in the Serbian language via a Serbian interpreter. At the same time the journalist conducted an interview also with Albanian number 1. The interviews were taken in the same room with all of us but we were responding the questions one by one." That's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, yes. That's perfectly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Deals with number 2 and the circumstances of number 1. Paragraph 9: "The interviews were taken by a male English speaking journalist at the presence of a cameraman and Serbian and English speaking interpreter. I do not remember the name of the English speaking journalist. Even if the ICTY investigator would tell me the name I am not able to confirm it as correct. Maybe I could recognise the person by face only. But I would like to stress that I did not give any other interview in Hotel Prague in Belgrade apart from this one. "In Hotel Prague were present plainclothes and uniformed Serbian Interior Ministry police officers." Pause there. You'll probably read on to the next line and we're coming to it, but just pausing there. In the hotel there were Serb Interior Ministry police officers present; correct?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But they were not present in the basement during the interview?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that clarifies, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does; yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A proper research method, ambiguity: Clarify it by going to a better source? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad you clarified what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this shows the value, doesn't it, of proper research methods?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You came to the same conclusion I did through my methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "I believe I was identified as an interview subject because of my ethnicity, combined with the fact that" -- I'm not going to read the last bit but you can read it.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that how he was identified?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He identified himself in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was he actually got to the Hotel Prague?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I don't know that answer. I know -- I know how the interview -- I know how I organised the interview but I don't know how he got to the Hotel Prague, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So someone on your behalf, to use the modern verb derived from a noun, targeted him as a potential interviewee.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Targeted. No, that's not accurate. Targeted, no, that's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 11: "I would like to say that, as with all interviews, I have responded to all questions in the manner that would have been expected from me by the Belgrade authorities ..." I'm sorry that you laugh, Mr. Lituchy. Explain, please, why it should be funny --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, listen to the question. Why it should be funny that a refugee in the state like the Belgrade state, or the Serbian state was in Belgrade at this time, should say something like that.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absurd when you think about the fact that this man's father was murdered by the KLA. How could -- how could -- how is it possible that he needed any compulsion to tell the truth or to speak? He was compelled by his own personal life experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Refugees in Belgrade at this time were in a hostile environment.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's absolutely false. That's totally false.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The government of this accused was not friendly to this type of refugee at all, was it?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In fact, I think the only thing that saved his life was that he did have this government to flee to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you feel it appropriate, when somebody interviewed about this experience sets it out, you think it appropriate to laugh, do you, at his assertion?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was laughing at you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's see exactly what it was you were laughing at. Your answer was with "targeted." You said that's not accurate. I asked you paragraph 11, and I quoted from the person being interviewed, and I quoted only so far. I got down to the word "Belgrade authorities," and then I interrupted myself because you were laughing. So explain to me how, Mr. Lituchy, since you volunteered this, how you find it appropriate to laugh at me when I read out verbatim the words of somebody interviewed last week in careful and considered circumstances about your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't -- I don't accept this as an accurate statement, and I think it's -- I think it's a terrible distortion of what actually happened, because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were laughing at the statement and the person being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And not at me.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're the one who said that it's the Belgrade authorities. Well, okay, you may have been reading from this statement, but I can't -- I can't accept this as being -- as being anything but some fraud.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, your bias and prejudice is such, and you revealed it, that you would laugh at a refugee.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At somebody upon who --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then let me ask you this question before we read on: You as a serious researcher, if somebody you've spoken to says something different and gives an explanation for why the account is different, do you consider it --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- or do you just laugh it off?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. This is just --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you laugh it off, Mr. Lituchy?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's read on and get to the end of this.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll take the same sentence again and you must feel free to respond in whatever way you think's appropriate. "I would like to say that, as with all interviews, I have responded to all questions in the manner that would have been expected from me by the Belgrade authorities - who approved the interview in the first place - and would in no way have criticised the Serbian government. "I am always mindful during the interview, of the fact that my family remained ... even though it was now ... more importantly, I was in in Belgrade where any negative statements towards the government as well as any support for the NATO action would in my opinion --" and then he sets out the consequences for himself and/or for others. He explained in paragraph 13 that he hasn't been approached by you or, until we approached him, by anyone. He explains his willingness to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honours, again, this is a clarification of and indeed a slight change from the position in the Sutch statement at paragraph 14 where he deals with the question of protection. I don't need to read that out but I certainly want the Chamber to have read it. And the Chamber will see in paragraph 14, in the second to last line, there is an amplification or addition to the grounds of his position of last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, Mr. Lituchy, were asking questions with your colleagues sitting around you and with an unreliable interpreter in circumstances that would bring about unreliable answers from those to whom you spoke.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Everything about Albanian number 3, and indeed everything about the rest of the circumstances of this interview and the transcript show that this is an unreliable document.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not -- that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that I can understand your position, you never interviewed those in Albania or Macedonia who had left Kosovo in the period either before or during the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only interviewed Roma refugees in Serbia and in Kosovo, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made one observation - this is I think my last question, or my last topic which may be two questions but no more - about those Serbs who left the Krajina, you described it in the most dramatic terms, and left for Belgrade. Are you aware that many of them were forced straight out into Kosovo without any sympathy being given to them by the Belgrade authorities?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact, but if -- if -- it's -- I don't know. I don't know the answer to that. I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions. With regard to the third Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we can see, he even gave some kind of a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry. Mr. Nice, do you wish to exhibit these?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question of exhibits, it's a fairly difficult one at the moment. There are two things that I would invite the Chamber at some stage to consider, and that is whether in relation to the production of whatever parts of the exhibit itself, the Chamber should consider Rule 95, which says that no evidence should be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to or could seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. The Chamber has now heard a great deal more evidence about this exhibit, including concessions by the witness himself as to the transcript. Of course they rely on the tape itself. If the Chamber admits the exhibit in part, clearly not in whole, but if it admits it in part, I would of course apply for the statement taken to go in as an exhibit, but I'm aware of what the Chamber's practice was in relation to an earlier witness. It's a matter that I'm seeking to resolve. I make no mystery of the fact that there's a motion or so coming your way today or, at the latest I hope, tomorrow, but I can hardly -- I can hardly consciously ask for something that I know to be inconsistent with your earlier and recent practice. The Prosecution's position is, however, that if the exhibit goes in of the witness, then, yes, the statement would be an item we would like to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript has already been admitted, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it probably has been, but, Your Honour, I'm quite sure that it's always possible for decisions about admissibility of documents to be changed, but that's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. Nice. Let's hear the re-examination, and bear in mind we're stopping at twenty past.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try not to keep Mr. Lituchy until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice provided two documents. There's no need to omit mentioning the name. That is Sutch, Jonathan Sutch who interviewed Albanian number 3. At the bottom of page 1 - and Mr. Nice indicated this- it says -- let me skip over this that this gentleman stated that another person, another important person from Kosovo, an Albanian: "[In English] ... interviews as well as plainclothed Serbian Interior Ministry police officers." [Interpretation] So the investigator claims that this Albanian number 3 said to him very decidedly that a policeman was present during the interview. In paragraph 10 of his statement that was quoted to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the statement. Sutch makes it clear later that the witness says that there was no one present from the police in the Hotel Prague interview, which is the only one that matters for this purpose. The position's already clear that the witness wasn't claiming there were any police present at that stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry Mr. Bonomy. Maybe I did not understand what it says here. It states here Mr. XY stated "[In English] Mr. XYZ would be present in the interviews as well as -- as well as plainclothed Serbian Ministry of Interior police officers." [Interpretation] Full stop. I'm reading what it says here towards the end of Mr. Sutch's statement. I cannot claiming or representing anything. I'm just reading out a part of the statement. This is the very bottom of page 1 of Mr. Sutch's statement, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the next sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next sentence doesn't have anything to do with any presence. "He does not recall -- [In English] police being present at the Hotel Prague interview." [Interpretation] It has to do with the following: "[In English]... that he was identified as an interview subject because of his -- of his ethnicity combined with the fact that he was --" then there is about profession. [Interpretation] So that is clear, I hope. Then in paragraph 10 of his statement, "In Hotel Prague "[In English] were present plainclothed and uniformed Serbian Interior Ministry police officers. But they were not present in the basement during the interview." [Interpretation] I have a question for Mr. Lituchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, on these tapes, these extensive tapes that you handed in and that were submitted here, is there any recording that depicts all the persons present in the room? Can you remember that? I, for example, cannot remember, but that's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. It does show -- it does show -- the camera does pan from right to left toward the end of the interview and it shows -- it doesn't pan from -- it does not pan from left to right, but it pans from right to left toward the end of the interview, showing the Romas in the left-hand corner of the room. That much I recall. It shows me as well, conducting the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what is the point of mentioning the possibility - I underline the word "possibility" - that some kind of plain clothed policeman was somewhere in a big hotel? Does that indicate any kind of police presence or the fact that in a big hotel like the Hotel Prague a person can find a policeman somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question put to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Did anybody say that to you? These are policemen in plain clothes here, did anyone say that to you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean that is -- that is why it seems absurd to me, because we certainly had no knowledge of any police anywhere near. In fact, for that matter, even in the entire hotel or even out in the street. Who knows where there were policemen. Somewhere in the city, I suppose. I don't know. But not in that hotel. Not in that room, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not in that room at any rate. That is your assertion. And whether there were any policemen in the hotel, that is not what you're saying at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I don't know. I mean, I -- I didn't -- I didn't see any policemen walking into the hotel or walking out of the hotel. So as far as I know, we know for a fact there was no one like that in the room, so -- and I didn't see anyone going in or going out of the hotel who I could recognise as a being a policeman, so -- and the whole idea that we -- that we had policemen with us while doing this interview strikes me as being bizarre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please look at paragraph 12. Now he says: "[In English] I was always mindful during the interview of the fact that my family remained in Kosovo, even though it was now under NATO/UN protection..."

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember reading that, but I don't know -- oh, here it is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He says that his family stayed back in Kosovo. "[In English] ... that I was in Belgrade where any negative statements towards the government as well as support for the NATO action would - in my opinion - have lead to cause me and my family serious harms." [Interpretation] Serious harms. If his family was in Kosovo, is it possible that what he says about the NATO bombing --

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's illogical. It's an illogical statement. Totally illogical. Shall I explain why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was fleeing from Kosovo, from KLA terror. So if he was fleeing into the -- if -- if there was a possibility that the Yugoslav state was a threat to him, why would he flee from terror into the arms of the Yugoslav state for protection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not going to exhibit a lack of discipline. There is another trial scheduled to commence shortly. We were told to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can I just use one more minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he'll have to come back. All right. Well, one minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, please let's not return him. It's not that I have that much left. Just one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point 7.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point 7 in the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same point 7. You were asked yesterday how come you claimed that this Albanian number 2 was killed, and this Albanian number 3 says that this person was killed in 2003 in Glodjane village, Stimlje municipality. You know that.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now finally, how do you explain paragraph 14? I'm just going to read out the second part because of time constraints. "[In English] ... I say that I would prefer --" [Interpretation] he's talking about the video footage of the interview. "[In English] I would prefer it is disclosed in closed session because of safety of my family, which is currently living in Kosovo. Otherwise, I have no objections to disclose it." [Interpretation] So, does he insist that this be in closed session or - I'm asking you, Mr. Robinson - whether we could play this in open session so that it could be seen. I hope that Mr. Nice is not opposed to this. "[In English] Otherwise, I have no other objections to disclose..." [Interpretation] Although I think that what he says about the safety and security of his own family is reason enough. So I'm not going to insist on this, of course. Did he deny a single word from his interview in this statement? Did he deny a single word from the interview that is a considerably long interview? Did you find any denial or anything that he refuted here?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not deny anything in his interview, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no reason to ask that. He was asked about the detail of his interview. He was asked about the circumstances of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Your very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This Albanian number 3, was he the interviewee who gave the longest answers with political explanations, although you did not insist on such lengthy answers?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lituchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lituchy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. Tomorrow we deal with the question of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number for this particular tab 1 and tab 2. I don't -- tab 2 is out, but it's tab 1. I don't think we've had a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's deal with everything tomorrow because we are very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
